hints.title: Keep the stated domain
hints.body: A counterexample must be a positive integer N greater than 6 and must fail the proposed representation.
hints.recap: It must satisfy the hypothesis and contradict the conclusion.
hints.pitfall: A number outside the stated domain cannot refute the claim.

recall.reminder: One allowed counterexample disproves a universal claim; the allowance is essential.

hints.title: Interpret non-prime correctly
hints.body: Integers greater than 1 which are not prime begin 4, 6, 8, 9, … . In this question, neither 1 nor a prime can be a summand.
hints.pitfall: Using 1 would violate the greater-than-1 condition.

recall.reminder: Preserve every part of a definition and its domain.

hints.title: List the remaining possible sums
hints.body: For each remaining candidate, list the unordered pairs whose entries satisfy the lower bound for an allowed summand. Test both entries for primality.
hints.recap: A failed existence claim requires ruling out every permitted pair.
hints.pitfall: One valid-looking summand cannot compensate for an invalid other summand.
hints.pause: Finish the pair checks and decide which in-domain candidates refute the claim.

recall.reminder: A failed existence claim requires ruling out every permitted pair.

solution:
N=5 is outside N>6 and therefore cannot be a counterexample.

N=7 is in the domain. Every permitted summand is at least 4, so two such summands total at least 8; 7 has no valid representation.

N=9 is also in the domain. With both summands at least 4, the only unordered pair is 4+5, but 5 is prime. Thus it has no valid representation either.

II and III only are counterexamples: G.
knowledgePattern: Check hypothesis and conclusion of proposed counterexamples
